name: connector-routing
description: Connector routing for diagrams and schematics: many orthogonal connectors at once with bend, length and crossing costs, negotiated congestion, rip-up and reroute, and nudging

items: Diagram and graph editors (flowcharts, UML, node editors, architecture diagrams) that need connectors which avoid the boxes, bend rarely, cross rarely and do not lie on top of each other, and that should update incrementally when the user drags a box.
Schematic and EDA-style tools, and generators for cable or wiring plans, where many nets share narrow channels and nets with more than two ports become Steiner trees.
Layout engines that run their own placement: the nudging step solves its separation constraints exactly, and also exports them as data for an engine that places segments itself.

If you need the plain shortest path on a general graph, use [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search); for agents that move over time and must not meet at all, [mapf-search](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search); for Pareto fronts on graphs other than routing scenes, [multiobjective-search](https://github.com/sunsided/multiobjective-search).

name: constraint-search
description: Finite-domain constraint satisfaction for puzzles and deduction games: check that a puzzle has one solution, give human-style hints and grade difficulty, infer hidden facts, with propagation, all-different reasoning, backtracking and solution counting

items: Puzzle generators and solvers (Sudoku and its variants, nonograms, Minesweeper, Kakuro, logic grids): uniqueness checks stop at the second solution, and the human-style rules grade difficulty by the costliest technique a solve needs and give the next hint step.

Tutoring, hint and explainable configuration tools, and small scheduling or allocation models: rules carry names, and `Trace::why_removed` says which deduction ruled a value out, so "why can't I choose this?" has an answer next to the solution.

Game AI with hidden information, such as card locations or unrevealed Minesweeper cells: the backbone gives the certain facts, marginals the probability of each value, and sampling draws consistent hidden states to plan with, without enumerating worlds by hand.
Embedded and `no_std` users: the core needs only `alloc`, and parallel search is an opt-in `std` feature.

For large industrial models, optimisation objectives or huge domains, use [OR-Tools CP-SAT](https://developers.google.com/optimization), [Gecode](https://www.gecode.org/) or a MIP solver. For search over the moves of an adversarial game, use [game-tree-search](https://github.com/sunsided/game-tree-search); for shortest paths and state-space search with costs, [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search); for planning when the outcomes of actions are uncertain, rather than facts hidden, [stochastic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/stochastic-search).

name: cost-partition
description: Saturated cost partitioning and its maximum over orders for admissible planning heuristics over arbitrary abstractions

items: Authors of optimal classical planners who have several abstraction heuristics (pattern databases, merge-and-shrink, Cartesian or their own) and want an admissible combination that is usually stronger than taking their maximum.
Researchers comparing cost partitioning strategies: the saturated cost function of every abstraction is exposed (`cost_functions`), and any type that implements `sas_plus::Abstraction` can take part.
Teams that plan on embedded hardware, since the crate is `no_std` and has a single dependency.

For the abstractions themselves, use [sas-plus](https://github.com/sunsided/sas-plus) (projections) and [merge-and-shrink](https://github.com/sunsided/merge-and-shrink); for landmark cost partitioning, LM-cut or operator counting, [planning-heuristics](https://github.com/sunsided/planning-heuristics), which also wraps this crate's heuristics for its `Heuristic` trait.

audience.text: Part of the [planning and search crates](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/); see also this crate's [overview page](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/crates/cost-partition/).

name: decoupled-search
description: Decoupled (star-topology) search for factored SAS+ planning: star factorings, cost-optimal and greedy search, dominance pruning and decoupled heuristics

items: Planning researchers working on star-topology decoupling, factoring selection or dominance pruning who want a readable implementation, cross-checked against explicit search, to build on or compare against.

Planner authors whose tasks fall apart into a center and many weakly interacting leaves (transport, multi-robot delivery, manufacturing cells), where explicit search spends most of its effort on interleavings of leaf moves.
Embedded and robotics teams that plan onboard: the crate builds for `no_std` targets.

Tasks without a useful star factoring gain nothing from decoupling; `Factoring::auto` then falls back to explicit search, and for explicit-state search on its own [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) is the better fit.

For the heuristics themselves on ordinary states, use [planning-heuristics](https://github.com/sunsided/planning-heuristics); for symbolic search over the same tasks, [symbolic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/symbolic-search).

name: evolutionary-planning
description: Evolutionary planning for no_std: genetic algorithms, evolution strategies, CMA-ES and multi-objective evolutionary search over plans, paths and trajectories

items: Robotics and control engineers who optimise trajectories or motion parameters online, where the objective is a black box or a simulation and gradients are not available.
Game AI and simulation developers who plan with rolling-horizon evolution over their own forward model, or who need a robustness score for temporal-logic (STL) requirements.
People with several competing objectives (time, energy, risk) who want a Pareto front from NSGA-II, NSGA-III or MOEA/D instead of a hand-tuned weighted sum.
Researchers who want reproducible, budget-exact runs of the reference algorithms on embedded or `no_std` targets.

For optimal shortest paths with a good heuristic, use [`heuristic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search); for exact Pareto-optimal paths on graphs, [`multiobjective-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/multiobjective-search); for sampling-based motion planning (RRT, PRM), [`sampling-planning`](https://github.com/sunsided/sampling-planning); and for coordinating many agents on a graph, [`mapf-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search).

name: game-tree-search
description: Adversarial game-tree search for computer opponents in board, card and turn-based games: minimax, negamax, alpha-beta, principal variation search, MTD(f), iterative deepening with transposition tables, expectimax and Monte Carlo tree search

items: **Game developers writing a computer opponent** for a two-sided, turn-based game: board games, card games, tactics and combat systems. The side to move belongs to the position, so turn orders by initiative or speed, where one side may act several times in a row, work as they are.

**Opponents that explain themselves or scale in difficulty**: a search returns the chosen move with its score, the expected line of play, and the alternatives with their scores or bounds, so a game can show what its opponent considered or pick a weaker move on purpose.

**Games with a frame or time limit**: a node or time budget stops iterative deepening with the best move found so far, and a reusable searcher allocates nothing per position once warm. The crate is `no_std`, so it also runs on consoles, handhelds and in WebAssembly.

audience.text: It is not for single-agent problems: for pathfinding, see [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search); for puzzles, including checking that a puzzle has a unique solution and grading it, see [constraint-search](https://github.com/sunsided/constraint-search). Games with hidden information, such as most trick-taking card games, search sampled deals of the hidden cards, one deal at a time; [constraint-search](https://github.com/sunsided/constraint-search) draws deals consistent with what a player has seen, and tells which cards are certain or likely.

name: heuristic-search
description: Explicit-state heuristic graph search: A*, weighted and anytime, bounded-suboptimal, bidirectional, incremental and real-time search

audience.text: Anyone who has a graph, or a problem that can be phrased as one, and needs a path through it: a planner that generates its states on the fly, a robot or a game character on a grid. The graph stays in your code; you describe it through small traits (`Successors`, and `Predecessors` for the bidirectional searches), pass the goal test and the heuristic as separate values, and get back a path, an outcome and the expansion counters. The crate knows nothing about PDDL, SAS+ or any other model, so domain-specific representations sit on top of it rather than in it.

It is also meant for comparing algorithms on the same problem: every search uses the same traits, budgets and statistics, so trying IDA* or Weighted A* instead of A* changes the call, not the problem description. Symbolic (BDD), multi-objective, stochastic and width-based search are out of scope.

name: mapf-search
description: Multi-agent pathfinding on grids and graphs: CBS with its improvements, CBS-TA, FOCBS, ECBS, ICTS, PBS, PIBT, PIBT*_T, M*, EPEA*, MAPF-LNS2 and multi-objective MO-CBS

items: Robotics and warehouse automation: fleets of mobile robots or AGVs on a grid or a roadmap graph that must reach their goals without collisions.
Game developers moving groups of units through tight corridors, where independent A\* per unit deadlocks or collides.

Researchers who want CBS and its improvements (prioritized conflicts, bypass, CG/DG/WDG heuristics, disjoint splitting) switchable one by one, next to ECBS, ICTS, PBS, M\* and EPEA\* on the same instance type.

Planners that trade off several costs per agent (time, energy, risk): MO-CBS returns every Pareto-optimal joint plan, using [multiobjective-search](https://github.com/sunsided/multiobjective-search) as its low level.

For a single agent, use [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) directly; for many connectors on a diagram that may cross at a cost rather than never meet, [connector-routing](https://github.com/sunsided/connector-routing) is the better fit.

name: merge-and-shrink
description: Merge-and-shrink abstraction heuristics for SAS+ planning, with DFP and SCC-DFP merging, label reduction and bisimulation shrinking

items: People building optimal planners or search algorithms in Rust who need a strong admissible heuristic; the heuristic search itself, A* and friends, lives in [`heuristic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search).
Researchers and students experimenting with abstraction heuristics, merge or shrink strategies, or cost partitioning, who want a small, readable, tested implementation to change and measure.
Anyone who needs a reference h* on small tasks: with exact bisimulation and `prune: false`, the result is perfect on every state, so it can check other heuristics.

To add several abstractions up admissibly, combine them with [`cost-partition`](https://github.com/sunsided/cost-partition); for delete-relaxation, landmark or red-black heuristics, use [`planning-heuristics`](https://github.com/sunsided/planning-heuristics) instead, and for exhaustive search over decision diagrams, [`symbolic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/symbolic-search).

audience.text: Without a size limit, exact bisimulation can still grow exponentially on large tasks. Set `max_states` (Fast Downward uses 50000) to bound every product; the heuristic stays admissible but is no longer perfect. The implementation favors readability over speed, so for large benchmarks Fast Downward remains much faster.

name: miniplan
description: Grounded classical PDDL planner library with breadth-first, A*, greedy best-first and bidirectional search and h^FF, h^add and h^max heuristics

items: Students and engineers learning classical planning, who want a planner small enough to read end to end, with the textbook searches and heuristics side by side.
Rust developers who need to solve small and medium PDDL tasks (puzzles, logistics, robot task sequencing) in-process, without shelling out to an external planner.
Researchers comparing forward, bidirectional and heuristic search on the same grounded task, with node counts and timings from `--stats`.

If you only need to parse, check or write PDDL, use [`pddl-rs`](https://github.com/sunsided/pddl-rs) directly. For heuristic search over your own graph rather than a PDDL task, see [`heuristic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search), and for width-based search without a heuristic, [`width-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/width-search).

audience.text: Part of the [planning and search crates](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/); see also this crate's [overview page](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/crates/miniplan/).

name: multiobjective-search
description: Multi-objective shortest paths over Pareto frontiers: BOA*, BOBA*, EMOA*, NAMOA*dr, A*pex and their approximate, anytime and parallel variants

items: Route planners that have to show the trade-off between two or more costs (fastest, shortest, cheapest, safest) rather than one "best" route, e.g. on road networks or grids.

Robotics and logistics people who need a bounded-suboptimal front quickly: the ε-approximate (BOA\*ε, PP-A\*, A\*pex) and anytime searches (A-BOA\*ε, A-A\*pex, TPA) trade front quality for time with a guaranteed factor.

Researchers comparing multi-objective search algorithms, who get the classic and recent algorithms behind one `Graph` interface, the standardized benchmark generators and a brute-force reference to test against.

For a single objective, [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) is the simpler and faster choice; for several agents that must not collide, [mapf-search](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search) (its MO-CBS uses this crate as the low level).

name: pddl
description: A PDDL 3.1 parser, strongly typed

items: Planner and tool authors who need to read PDDL in Rust and would rather match on typed goal descriptions and effects than walk an S-expression tree.

People writing or teaching PDDL, who get a language server for their editor ([`pddl-lsp`](https://github.com/sunsided/pddl-rs/tree/main/pddl-lsp)) and a validator that explains why a plan fails ([`pddl-validate`](https://github.com/sunsided/pddl-rs/tree/main/pddl-validate)).
Rust developers who ship PDDL with their program and want syntax errors to fail the build, or a domain compiled into typed planning code instead of interpreted at run time.
Researchers who want Fast Downward's `output.sas` format from PDDL without leaving Rust, for example to feed [`sas-plus`](https://github.com/sunsided/sas-plus) heuristics.
If you want a planner rather than a parser, [`miniplan`](https://github.com/sunsided/miniplan) grounds and solves PDDL tasks on top of this crate.

name: pddl-validate
description: Independent PDDL plan validator: classical, numeric and temporal plans with precise diagnostics

siblings.name: pddl-codegen
siblings.description: Generates typed Rust planning code from PDDL domains, for pddl's #[task] attribute and build scripts

siblings.name: pddl-core
siblings.description: The types and the parser behind the pddl crate; depend on pddl instead

siblings.name: pddl-lsp
siblings.description: A language server for PDDL: diagnostics, navigation, completion and formatting

siblings.name: pddl-macros
siblings.description: Compile-time checked PDDL: domain!, problem! and pddl! macros for the pddl crate

siblings.name: pddl-runtime
siblings.description: The planning-task trait, fact storage and reference searches that code generated from PDDL builds on

audience.text: An independent plan validator for PDDL: a second opinion next to [VAL](https://github.com/KCL-Planning/VAL), with precise, machine-readable diagnostics.

It is part of the [pddl-rs](https://github.com/sunsided/pddl-rs) workspace and depends only on the `pddl` syntax tree. It implements the validation semantics itself and shares no grounding or search code with any planner, so it does not share their bugs either.

let domain = Domain::from_str( "(define (domain switch) (:predicates (on)) (:action flip :parameters () :precondition (not (on)) :effect (on)))", ).unwrap(); let problem = Problem::from_str( "(define (problem light) (:domain switch) (:init) (:goal (on)))", ).unwrap(); let validator = Validator::new(&domain, &problem).unwrap();

let report = validator.validate_text("(flip)\n(flip)"); assert_eq!(report.status(), ValidationStatus::Invalid); assert_eq!( report.violation().unwrap().advice(), "(flip) has an unsatisfied precondition at step 2: (Set (on) to false)" ); ```

name: planning-heuristics
description: Heuristics for classical planning: delete relaxation (h_max, h_add, h_FF), red-black, landmarks, LM-cut, operator counting and abstraction adapters

items: Planning researchers who want to compare heuristics on the same task representation without porting Fast Downward's C++, or who need a reference implementation of red-black planning or RHW landmarks to check their own against.

Anyone building a classical planner in Rust: pick `h_FF` or red-black for satisficing greedy search, LM-cut or landmark cost partitioning for optimal A*, and LAMA-style landmark tracking for path-dependent search.
Embedded and robotics teams that plan onboard: the crate runs on `no_std` targets with an allocator.

If the problem is a plain graph rather than a factored planning task, an explicit-state search with a domain-specific heuristic in [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) is the better fit.

For merge-and-shrink abstractions or saturated cost partitioning themselves, use [merge-and-shrink](https://github.com/sunsided/merge-and-shrink) and [cost-partition](https://github.com/sunsided/cost-partition); this crate only adapts them to the `Heuristic` trait.

name: planning-qubo
description: Planning, scheduling and constraint problems as QUBO and Ising models: encoders, decoders, penalty tuning, classical samplers and export for quantum annealers

items: **Anyone who wants a planning problem as a QUBO or Ising model.** Encoders turn assignment, constraint satisfaction, time-indexed scheduling, multi-agent path finding and routing problems into models, and decoders map a sample back to a plan and name each violated constraint. The penalty builder covers other problems with the same constraints (exactly-one, at-most-one, linear with slack bits), and `penalty` picks the weights. The models feed any QUBO solver: the samplers here, quantum-inspired hardware, or a quantum annealer.

**Researchers comparing samplers on the same model.** The exhaustive sampler gives the exact optimum of small models. Simulated annealing, tabu search and parallel tempering, each with a seeded RNG, show how close a heuristic gets. All of them stop on a work budget and resume later, so runs can be time-sliced and measured by the work they did. `sample_parallel` runs several at once.

**People with access to a D-Wave annealer.** The `dwave` module writes models in the Solver API's format and reads the returned samples back for the decoders. Submitting them over the network is left to a separate adapter.
**Exact experiments and teaching.** `i64` models keep every penalty and every QUBO-to-Ising conversion exact, so results can be checked against brute force.

audience.text: It is not for solving these problems fast on a classical machine. A direct solver beats a QUBO encoding there: see [task-allocation](https://github.com/sunsided/task-allocation) for assignment, [constraint-search](https://github.com/sunsided/constraint-search) for constraint satisfaction, [mapf-search](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search) for multi-agent path finding and [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) for pathfinding.

name: polyzonotope
description: Sparse polynomial zonotopes, zonotopes and interval boxes for set-based reachability analysis, no_std and optionally with outward rounding

audience.text: This crate does set-based reachability analysis with sparse polynomial zonotopes: rather than simulating one state at a time, it pushes a whole set of possible states through a model, and the result always encloses every state the system can actually reach. This is useful whenever the state is not known exactly. A drone, a robot arm or a cruise controller has sensors that are slightly off, a payload somewhere between 2 and 3 kg, and wind acting on it; a simulation with the best guess yields one trajectory, while the question for safety is where the system could *possibly* end up, for every value the uncertain parts might take. If none of those states lies inside the wall, the system cannot hit it; if one does, it is better to find out on paper.

This is the counterpart to sampling-based planners such as rapidly-exploring random trees (RRT). An RRT grows a tree of single trajectories until one of them reaches the goal, so it finds *a* way there, assuming everything happens exactly as computed. Reachability asks the opposite question: whether *any* of the possible outcomes is unsafe. The two combine well, since the planner proposes a path and the reachable set of the system following it shows that the path stays safe under the uncertainty.
How well that works depends on how the set is described. This crate has three descriptions, from coarse to fine:

items: An interval box is one range per axis ("x between 1 and 2, y between 0 and 5"). It is cheap, but it loses shape quickly: rotate a box and you have to wrap the rotated box in a new, bigger one; repeated over many steps, this wrapping effect makes the box far larger than the set inside it.

A zonotope is a center plus a few direction vectors, each stretched by some amount between -1 and 1. It can be skewed and stays exact under rotations, scaling and sums, so linear models don't blow it up.

A sparse polynomial zonotope also allows those amounts to be multiplied with each other and raised to powers. That gives curved shapes (the parabola in the example below is one), and it keeps track of which uncertain quantity is which: two sets derived from the same sensor reading stay linked, instead of each pretending the other could take any value.

audience.text: The crate is `no_std` with `alloc`, forbids `unsafe`, and with the `sound` feature rounds every enclosure outward, so its proofs hold in floating point too. Its main operations are cross-checked against [CORA](https://github.com/TUMcps/CORA), the MATLAB toolbox for reachability analysis.

name: polyzonotope-reach
description: Validated reachable-set over-approximation of linear and nonlinear dynamics with sparse polynomial zonotopes

items: Anyone who needs to know where a dynamical system could end up for every value its uncertain parts might take: an initial state known only to a set, inputs that can be any signal inside a zonotope.
Linear systems `x' = A x + B u` go through `LinearReach`; nonlinear ones `x' = f(x, u)` through `NonlinearReach`, by conservative linearization or polynomialization, with adaptive step sizes.
Each step returns the states at the end of the step and every state the system can pass through during it, so a set can be checked against obstacles over the whole time span.

The sets are the sparse polynomial zonotopes of [`polyzonotope`](https://github.com/sunsided/polyzonotope); [`robust-planning`](https://github.com/sunsided/robust-planning) uses them to check planned motions under bounded uncertainty.

name: quantum-planning
description: Quantum algorithms for planning and search, on simulators: Grover search, quantum backtracking, amplitude estimation, quantum walks on game trees and QAOA

items: **Researchers, students and teachers of quantum speedups for search**: exact Grover search with a known number of solutions and BBHT exponential search with an unknown number, on a state-vector simulator. The oracle is an ordinary validity check on a candidate, such as "is this plan valid", so the same predicate serves a classical and a quantum search.

**Honest query-count comparisons**: every phase-oracle application and every classical check of a measured candidate counts as one query. Put these counts next to a classical scan over the same oracle, and the `√N` against `N` gap shows on real instances, not only in the formula.
**`no_std` demos**: the crate needs only `alloc`, so it runs in WebAssembly, for example in a browser page that shows the amplitudes change from one Grover iteration to the next.

audience.text: It is a simulator: its memory doubles with each qubit and stops at 24 qubits, so it finds no solution faster than a classical search does. To solve plans, use [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) for state-space search, [constraint-search](https://github.com/sunsided/constraint-search) for constraint problems and [game-tree-search](https://github.com/sunsided/game-tree-search) for two-player games.

name: resource-timeline
description: Resource timelines for onboard scheduling: energy, memory, thermal and communication budgets with explained violations, envelopes and allocation-free storage

items: Flight software and mission operations engineers who place activities on a spacecraft or rover and need to know whether battery, memory, data volume, instruments or comm windows hold up, onboard or on the ground before uplink.
Developers of onboard or embedded schedulers that need checked arithmetic, explicit budgets and no heap.
Planners and replanners that want a violation explained (the tick, the level and the activities involved) instead of a bare "infeasible".

Game AI and simulation developers whose agents spend stamina, ammunition, storage or build capacity over game ticks, as in colony, strategy and survival games. Earliest-start search answers when an agent can afford an action, interval claims model shared workstations and cooldowns, end-state targets check a build order against a scouted attack, and the allocation-free variants keep checks off the heap inside a frame. See [`examples/colony.rs`](https://github.com/sunsided/resource-timeline/blob/main/examples/colony.rs) and [`examples/rush.rs`](https://github.com/sunsided/resource-timeline/blob/main/examples/rush.rs).

For the timing side of the same schedule (whether its temporal constraints can be met under uncertain durations, and executing it), use [temporal-control](https://github.com/sunsided/temporal-control). The two crates share only a convention (`i64` ticks, half-open intervals) and no dependency, because temporal controllability does not imply resource safety and both checks have to run.

name: robust-planning
description: Motion planning over reachable sets under bounded uncertainty: Robust-RRT, Robust RRT* and reachability-guided A* with conservative safety proofs

items: Engineers working on autonomous vehicles, drones or spacecraft who have a dynamics model with bounded noise and need a path that is safe for the whole tube around it, not only for the nominal trajectory.
Researchers in set-based verification who want to put their reachability analysis behind RRT, RRT* or a lattice search without writing the planner first.
Anyone who already plans with sampling-planning and wants its RRT, PRM or BIT* to accept only proven-safe edges in Euclidean spaces (`ReachChecker`).
You bring the `Reach` model, i.e. the propagation of a set along one edge; the crate ships the planners, obstacles, goals and containment tests around it.

When the dynamics are deterministic and a collision check on single states is enough, [sampling-planning](https://github.com/sunsided/sampling-planning) alone is simpler and much faster; for uncertainty in the action outcomes of a discrete model (MDPs, POMDPs), [stochastic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/stochastic-search) is the better fit.

name: sampling-planning
description: Sampling-based motion planning for no_std: RRT, RRT*, RRT-Connect, PRM, SPARS, FMT*, BIT*, AIT*, SST and KPIECE

items: Robotics engineers who need a path for an arm, a mobile base or a car-like vehicle through a continuous space with obstacles, and who bring their own collision checker.
Vehicles with a turning radius: the Dubins and Reeds-Shepp spaces plan along the actual shortest car paths, not along straight lines that are fixed up afterwards.
Systems that can only be forward-simulated (no steering function, just "apply this control for that long"): SST, SST* and KPIECE work over a `Propagator` instead.
Anyone comparing planners on the same problem; the bundled example runs eleven of them on one world and draws the results.
Embedded and other `no_std` targets with an allocator, and test setups that need reproducible runs.

For discrete graphs and grids, [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) is the better fit; for many robots sharing one map, [mapf-search](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search); for dynamics with bounded disturbances where the plan has to hold for every reachable state, [robust-planning](https://github.com/sunsided/robust-planning).

name: sas-plus
description: SAS+ / finite-domain planning tasks compatible with Fast Downward's translator, with labeled transition systems, projections and test oracles

audience.text: `sas-plus` provides building blocks for planning heuristics and search in Rust, in the spirit of crates like `tower`: small pieces you can reason about one at a time. It is not a planner itself, but meant for people who write or test such algorithms.

`Task` and `LabeledTransitionSystem` are plain structs with public fields: a task is its variables, operators, initial state, goal and axioms, and a transition system is a list of labeled transitions with a goal flag per state. The one abstraction on top is the `Abstraction` trait, which maps a concrete state to a state of a transition system; anything that implements it, a `Projection` or a type of your own, can stand in wherever a heuristic needs abstract goal distances. The crate has no required dependencies and is `no_std`; it only needs `alloc`.

For testing, `Task::perfect_heuristic()` computes the exact goal distance h\* on small tasks, and `random::random_task` generates reproducible tasks from a seed, so a heuristic can be checked against h\* over as many seeds as you care to run. On top of that, the `fdr` module reads Fast Downward's translator output, which brings real benchmark domains in without writing a grounder.
There is no search algorithm and no PDDL parser. To ground PDDL into a SAS+ task, the `sas-plus` feature of [`pddl`](https://github.com/sunsided/pddl-rs) does that.

name: search-core
description: Shared cost, heuristic, goal and budget traits for search and planning crates, with exact no_std cost types

items: Authors of search and planning crates who want their algorithms to accept the same heuristics, goal tests and budgets as the other crates of the ecosystem, instead of defining yet another `Heuristic` trait.

Users of those crates who write a domain heuristic (a grid distance, a pattern database, a relaxed-plan estimate) or a goal test once and pass it to every algorithm that takes the shared trait for that cost type, such as the A\* family of heuristic-search or the MDP planners of stochastic-search (which use `f64` costs).
Anyone who needs exact path costs, e.g. prices or durations with a fixed number of decimal places, or lexicographic costs such as "fewest steps, then fewest conflicts".

If you are looking for an actual search algorithm rather than the traits, pick [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) for A* and its relatives, [multiobjective-search](https://github.com/sunsided/multiobjective-search) for Pareto fronts, [mapf-search](https://github.com/sunsided/mapf-search) for multi-agent pathfinding or [stochastic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/stochastic-search) for MDPs and POMDPs.

audience.text: Part of the [planning and search crates](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/); see also this crate's [overview page](https://sunsided.github.io/planning-and-search/crates/search-core/).

name: stochastic-search
description: Planning under probabilistic outcomes for MDPs and POMDPs: LAO*, iLAO*, CG-iLAO*, RTDP, LRTDP, BRTDP, FRTDP, VPI-RTDP, POMCP, DESPOT and multi-objective MOLAO*, iMOLAO* and MOLRTDP

items: Robotics and autonomy work where actions have uncertain outcomes and the planner needs a policy with a convergence guarantee (LRTDP, iLAO\*) or with bounds on how far it is from optimal (BRTDP, FRTDP, VPI-RTDP).

Online decision making under partial observability, e.g. a robot or game agent acting on noisy sensor readings, where POMCP or DESPOT plan from a particle belief and reuse their search tree between decisions.
Planning with several competing costs (time against risk, energy against wear), where the multi-objective algorithms return the convex coverage set of policies instead of one weighted compromise.
Researchers and students comparing MDP heuristic search algorithms on the same model and test oracle.

If every action has exactly one outcome, use [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) (or [multiobjective-search](https://github.com/sunsided/multiobjective-search) for several costs); it is simpler and much faster. Goal tests written against [search-core](https://github.com/sunsided/search-core) work in both, and heuristics carry over once their cost type is `f64`.

name: symbolic-search
description: Symbolic search for SAS+ planning with BDDs: symbolic BFS and Dijkstra, bidirectional search, BDDA*, SymBA* and symbolic abstraction heuristics

items: Planning researchers working on cost-optimal planning who want BDD-based search (SymBA\*, BDDA\*, symbolic PDBs, symbolic merge-and-shrink) on the same task representation as the other planning crates, without wrapping Gamer or Fast Downward's symbolic search.
Planner authors who need optimal plans, or a proof that no plan exists, on tasks whose state spaces are too large for explicit search but regular enough for compact BDDs.

Anyone experimenting with transition-relation partitioning (disjunctive groups, conjunctive clusters with greedy or IWLS95 schedules) or variable orders, with a reference BDD to check results against.

For explicit-state heuristic search, use [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) with heuristics from [planning-heuristics](https://github.com/sunsided/planning-heuristics); for tasks that factor into a center and loosely coupled leaves, [decoupled-search](https://github.com/sunsided/decoupled-search) is often the better fit.

name: task-allocation
description: Decentralized multi-agent task allocation: consensus-based bundle algorithm (CBBA) and auctions that converge to conflict-free assignments over delayed, intermittent communication

items: Robot and rover teams, drone swarms and multi-agent simulations that split tasks without a central planner, over links that drop and delay messages. CBBA settles on a conflict-free assignment from whatever each agent hears, and the seeded network simulator tests that before deployment.
Games and simulations that hand out jobs to workers, units or NPCs, where a job's value depends on what the agent already holds. Integer scores and the seeded simulator keep runs deterministic.
Researchers comparing allocation algorithms: CBBA, auctions and sequential greedy run on the same valuations, next to an exhaustive optimum for small instances.

For plain one-to-one assignment with all state in one process, the Hungarian algorithm (for example `kuhn_munkres` in the [pathfinding](https://crates.io/crates/pathfinding) crate) is enough. Timing constraints between agents fit [temporal-control](https://github.com/sunsided/temporal-control), shared resource budgets [resource-timeline](https://github.com/sunsided/resource-timeline), and travel costs can come from [heuristic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) or [sampling-planning](https://github.com/sunsided/sampling-planning).

name: temporal-control
description: Simple temporal networks with uncertainty: dynamic controllability checking, dispatchable networks and a no_std, no-alloc onboard dispatcher

items: Flight software and robotics engineers who schedule activities with uncertain durations on a spacecraft, rover or robot and need the timing checked before uplink and executed onboard without a heap. The design targets adoption by an existing executive such as F Prime or cFS.
Planners that emit temporal plans and need to know whether the plan stays executable under duration uncertainty, with an explanation when it does not.

Researchers comparing dynamic controllability algorithms: Morris 2014, RUL⁻, RUL2021, the labelled closure and a per-label backpropagation run on the same networks and are cross-checked against each other and a brute-force oracle.

For energy, memory, thermal or communication budgets over the same timeline, [resource-timeline](https://github.com/sunsided/resource-timeline) is the companion crate; for durations with probabilities rather than bounds, [stochastic-search](https://github.com/sunsided/stochastic-search) is the better fit.

name: width-search
description: Width-based search without heuristics: novelty tables, Iterated Width (IW), hierarchical IW, IHIW, π-HIW, Serialized IW, SIW+, SIW-R with sketches, BFWS, Rollout IW and π-IW for planning and games

items: Planning and search people who want IW, SIW or BFWS in Rust, on SAS+ tasks or on their own state representation, without writing a heuristic first.

Game and tool developers who need to check that a generated level is solvable, plan for NPCs from world-state facts, or explore a simulator from its raw state bytes (more in [In games](https://github.com/sunsided/width-search#in-games)).
Researchers comparing novelty-based pruning against heuristic search, with node counts that line up with LAPKT.

For shortest paths with action costs and a good distance heuristic, A* and its variants in [`heuristic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/heuristic-search) are the better pick. Heuristics for classical planning tasks live in [`planning-heuristics`](https://github.com/sunsided/planning-heuristics), and probabilistic outcomes are handled by [`stochastic-search`](https://github.com/sunsided/stochastic-search).
